messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Donald, a 73-year-old divorced journalist of North American background, sought help after years of trying to keep his world manageable by making it smaller. The traumatic event dated back to a man-made disaster he had covered as a reporter, when he was sent into the aftermath of a public attack that left smoke, shattered glass, sirens, and panicked survivors crowding the streets. In the immediate confusion he had noticed the taste of something metallic and bitter in his mouth and, decades later, that same taste could still jolt him back with startling force. Photographs from the scene were especially potent: if an image resembled the broken storefronts, bodies, or police tape from that day, he would feel his stomach tighten and his attention lock onto exits, hands, and anything that might be used as a weapon. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself to think about it, he would not be able to handle what came up; the event felt so extreme that parts of it seemed unreal, as if it had happened to someone else, and yet he also feared that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore and that he would never feel normal emotions again. Even now, a sudden shift in a crowd, an unexpected knock at his apartment door, or a glimpse of a related photo could leave him rigid, scanning for danger, and reaching automatically for habits that made him feel less exposed: he always chose a seat with his back to the wall so he could see the room, and he would freeze completely if he felt threatened, as if any movement might make things worse. Those same trigger moments fed his conviction that the event could return at any time, which made him listen for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home and keep himself on edge in any safe place, unable to relax. Because he expected danger, he noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects in every environment, from a kitchen knife in a friend’s apartment to a metal rod in a subway repair area, and the constant scanning made ordinary places feel contaminated by the possibility of attack.

Over time, Donald’s efforts to keep fear at bay began to reshape the way his memory worked. When he sat with his back against a wall or kept his ears tuned for footsteps outside his door, he found that the disaster would surface in fragments with unusual force: the memory replayed like a film on loop, and when he remembered it he felt as though it were happening right now. The more he froze, watched, and listened, the more these scenes returned unbidden, and each return seemed to confirm that the memory was not over but waiting just beneath the surface. He would then think again that he could not bear to think about it, that he would never be normal again, and that his life had lost its meaning. Those appraisals pushed him back into the same routines: he sat with his back to the wall in restaurants and waiting rooms, checked locks repeatedly, and spent money impulsively on unnecessary things to distract or comfort himself after a trigger left him rattled. His days narrowed around these habits, and he became less willing to visit busy places or accept invitations that might place him somewhere unpredictable. Yet the more he controlled his surroundings, the more sensitive he became to signs of risk; a related photograph in a newspaper archive, a sudden noise in the hallway, or the metallic aftertaste that followed stress would quickly bring the disaster back to mind and revive the sense that another catastrophe might be unfolding. In his work as a journalist, even though he was semi-retired, he still read and edited from home, and the unpredictability of breaking news alerts or an unscheduled call could send him into that same alert state, listening for intrusion and scanning the room as though danger might step through the door. Donald’s divorce years earlier had left him living alone, which made the silence of his apartment especially hard to tolerate because it gave him more time to hear the imagined approach of someone entering, more time to notice every sharp object in sight, and more time for the old scene to flood back with the force of now.

By the time he came for help, Donald described a life organized around trying not to be overwhelmed, yet feeling overwhelmed anyway. He was most afraid that if he allowed himself to remember fully, he would break down and never recover; at the same time, he hoped that if he could learn to face the memory without being swallowed by it, he might reclaim some sense that his remaining years still mattered.
